## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Siṅgālajātaka* (Ja 148), titled *The Jackal*, is a narrative text preserved in the Pali Jātaka collection. According to its traditional framing story, the Buddha related this discourse while residing at Jetavana on the subject of subduing desires, illustrated by the proverb "Once bitten, twice shy". In modern studies of the early Saṅgha, Ja 148 is referenced as textual evidence for the personal duties of the venerable Ānanda, who acted as an attendant to the Buddha and was responsible for summoning the monks together, occasionally even at midnight [Nyanaponika et al. 2003].

In the tale of the past, the Bodhisattva was reborn as a tree-spirit dwelling in a cemetery grove [DeCaroli 1999]. The narrative features a festival celebrated in honor of spirit-deities, during which meat and fish were strewn across the streets of a city and jars of alcohol were placed outside [DeCaroli 1999]. While the Bodhisattva tree-spirit showed no interest in the proceedings, a cunning jackal seized the opportunity to consume the food and drink [DeCaroli 1999]. This narrative is uniquely noted as the only Jātaka to describe this particular festival in detail, though depictions of spirit-deities receiving meat and alcohol offerings appear frequently across the wider Jātaka corpus [DeCaroli 1999].
